Reflecting on Lab 1 and the start of MicroPs!





Sep 3, 2025


Tali Smith












Initial Reflections Post


I’m very excited to be taking MicroPs this semester! I wanted to take this class because I really enjoyed E85, particularly the portion where we used the FPGA. I found that the labs were much more interesting than the problem sets, so I’m excited to be taking a course with only labs. Some of my goals would be to become more comfortable using FPGAs, and understanding more thoroughly terminology distinctions (such as microprocessors vs microcontrollers), and become super familiar with git.

title: Lab 2 Report
Lab 2 Report
text: Figure 1 shows the overall block diagram of Lab 2’s design. The design has four modules: top, selectDisplay, switchSum, sevenSegment, (and the top module also uses HSOSC).

title: Lab 2 Report
text: The physical layout of the hardware for Lab 2 is shown by Figure 2 above. Notably, only 4 of the switches were physically on the breadboard, and the 4 DIP switches that were connected to the board and used were not included in this schematic. The FPGA was connected to a dual seven-segment display, as well as 5 LEDs.

title: Lab 2 Report
text: Testbenches were created for all the modules.  The top module was the most complex, because it had the most inputs and outputs to check. My code passed the testbench!  The next most complex module was the selectDisplay module. Working with the clock proved to be challenging, especially in understanding how to simulate the clock. Eventually, I was able to pass this testbench as well!  The switchSum module was the simplest, it actually only had one line of code! It is essentially just an adder.  The sevenSegment module was pretty much identical to the sevenSegment module from last week’s lab. The only difference in the module itself is that I now put it in its own file. Additionally, I didn’t have time for the testbench last week, so now I can actually prove it works in simulation.

title: Lab 2 Report
text:
My code worked in simulation and in hardware! I tested the testbenches first, and then tried the actual hardware. I did have some challenges implementing the hardware (turns out I had a couple of bad solders).
My design meets all of the requirements, and I believe I also met all of the “excellence” specs. The four PCB switches in combination with the 4 breadboard control the left and right display. The displays show independent numbers, without any noticeable bleeding or flickering. Additionally, the sum of these two numbers is represented in binary by 5 green LEDs on my breadboard.
This lab took a total of about 19 hours. I was somewhat expecting this lab to take less time than the last lab, but I guess everything takes longer than you expect. Nothing in this lab took particularly long by itself, it was just the sum of everything. I think the testbenches probably took the longest amount of time, with debugging the hardware coming in second, and writing the initial verilog was probably the fastest.

title: Lab 2 Report
text:
After pasting the initial prompt into ChatGPT, it returned code which I synthesized. This code synthesized on the first try. After last week’s success, I wasn’t too shocked by this, but still somewhat impressed. Some components were noticeably different from my implementation. Syntax-wise, all the code was in one file, and it wrote tons of comments, pretty much a comment per line. Additionally, instead of toggling the displays back and forth, it also included a part of the cycle that toggled them both off which I thought was interesting, and I’m curious as to why it chose to do that.
Interestingly, after giving ChatGPT my seven segment module code, and asking it to write the code based off of that, that code did not synthesize first try. I was surprised by this, especially considering it worked when it came up with its own code completely from scratch. Also, I know that my code is not the problem because it worked on lab 1 and 2. I wonder if, in general, it is more effective for ChatGPT to completely write its own code rather than modify existing code.

title: Lab 2 Report
Week 1 Reflection
text:
This week in lab was stressful! The unfamiliarity with the tools was definitely a challenge. I can’t believe I made it so long at Mudd without learning to use Git. Although I still feel pretty shaky with it, I think I’m becoming more comfortable with it.
Although I’m someone who normally strives for “excellence” in my coursework, I think I would enjoy this class a lot more if I let go of some of the perfectionist tendencies. I hope this course will help me learn when to stop working, and to be ok not reaching 100% of specs. I think this is already happening, considering I didn’t meet all the specs for Lab 1!
The part of this lab that I enjoyed the most was definitely writing the Verilog. I liked mapping what hex numbers were represented by different combinations of the switches, and then which A-G segments should light up for each. My least favorite part of the lab was going through the tutorials, although necessary, not as interesting. The good part is that I assume there won’t be many more tutorials, so each lab from now on will just be the fun part.
